'''Angel Chua Alcala''' {{post-nominals|post-noms=[[National Scientist of the Philippines|ONS]]}} (March 1, 1929 – February 1, 2023) was a Filipino biologist who was named a [[National Scientist of the Philippines]] in 2014. Alcala is known for his fieldwork to build [[Animal sanctuary|sanctuaries]] and to promote [[biodiversity]] in the [[aquatic ecosystem]]s of the Philippines. He was the Chairman of the Board of Advisers at the Angelo King Center for Research and Environmental Management located in [[Silliman University]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Angelo King Center for Research and Environmental Management {{!}} Silliman University |url=https://su.edu.ph/academics/centers-institutes/angelo-king-center-for-research-and-environmental-management/ |website=Silliman University}}</ref> Alcala published more than 200 peer-reviewed articles and books and his biological contributions to the environment and ecosystems have made him a renowned figure of natural sciences in the Philippines.<ref name="Silliman University">{{cite news |title=Dr. Alcala is One of First Filipinos Inducted into Fulbright Hall of Fame |url=http://su.edu.ph/dr-alcala-is-one-of-first-filipinos-inducted-into-fulbright-hall-of-fame/ |publisher=Silliman University |date=April 5, 2018}}</ref>

==Early life==
Alcala was born on March 1, 1929, in the municipality of [[Cauayan, Negros Occidental]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Angel Alcala |url=https://www.famousscientists.org/angel-alcala/ |website=www.famousscientists.org}}</ref> He was raised by a moderately low-income family in the small coastal town of Caliling, Philippines. Alcala worked alongside his father who worked as a fisherman at the nearby agricultural fish ponds.<ref name="Study.com">{{cite web |last1=Haak |first1=Danielle |title=Angel Alcala: Discoveries & Contribution to Biology |url=https://study.com/academy/lesson/angel-alcala-discoveries-contribution-to-biology.html |website=Study.com }}</ref> Due to his family's financial struggles, they depended on the ocean for its resources either<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Troxell|first=Eleanor|date=May 1936|title=The Unit-Activity Reading Series: Tom's Trip. Nina Benton Smith The Unit-Activity Reading Series: At Home and Away. Nila Banton Smith The Unit-Activity Reading Series: In City and Country. Nila Banton SmithThe Unit-Activity Reading Series: Round about You. Nina Benton SmithThe Unit-Activity Reading Series: Teachers' Guide for the First Year. Nila Banton Smith|journal=The Elementary School Journal|volume=36|issue=9|pages=712–714|doi=10.1086/457399|issn=0013-5984}}</ref> in providing food or items to sell.

==Education==
In 1951, Angel Alcala earned his bachelor's degree in biology ([[magna cum laude]]) from [[Silliman University]]. He then declined acceptance to the University of the Philippines College of Medicine in order to assist his family.<ref name="SoftSchools">{{cite web |title=Angel Alcala Facts |url=http://www.softschools.com/facts/scientists/angel_alcala_facts/930/ |website=www.softschools.com}}</ref> During that time, he occasionally assisted in biological fieldwork, for example for [[Sidney Dillon Ripley]] and [[Dioscoro Rabor]] in 1953 when they collected the only known (as of 2019) specimen of the [[Negros fruit dove]]. Alcala later attended [[Stanford University]] to complete his master's degree after 9 years. By 1966, he earned his Ph.D. in the same field and an honor doctorate from both the [[Xavier University]] and the [[University of Southeastern Philippines]]. Alcala later became a [[professor]] at [[Silliman University]], where he also served as president for two consecutive years. He served as secretary of the [[Department of Environment and Natural Resources]] from 1992 to 1995 and chairman of the [[Commission on Higher Education (Philippines)|Commission on Higher Education]] (CHEd) from 1995 to 1999.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://newsinfo.inquirer.net/628386/aquino-confers-awards-on-four-new-national-scientists |title=Who are the 4 new National Scientists of PH? |last=Sabillo |first=Kristine Angeli |date=August 12, 2014 |access-date=August 25, 2014 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812185818/http://newsinfo.inquirer.net/628386/aquino-confers-awards-on-four-new-national-scientists |archivedate=August 12, 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref> He also served as consultant on marine and aquatic projects under the [[United Nations Environment Programme]], [[World Bank]], [[Asian Development Bank]], World Bank Global Environment Facility, the Pew Fellowship in Marine Conservation, and the [[University of the Philippines]] [[Marine Science Institute, University of the Philippines|Marine Science Institute]].

==Research==
===Environmental management===
Angel Alcala is accredited with many research accomplishments and improvements regarding [[environmental management]], marine conservation, and discovery of new species. One of Alcala's works consisted of restoring or preserving areas with predominant wild, large predatory fish populations near a small [[marine sanctuary]] at [[Apo Island]] in the Philippines. His goal was to sustain hospitable conditions in this sanctuary throughout the duration of his research.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Russ |first1=Garry R. |last2=Alcala |first2=Angel C.|date=February 29, 1996|title=Do marine reserves export adult fish biomass? Evidence from Apo Island, central Philippines|journal=Marine Ecology Progress Series|volume=132|pages=1–9 |doi=10.3354/meps132001| bibcode=1996MEPS..132....1R|doi-access=free}}</ref> This sanctuary, called the Sumilon Marine Reserve, began as just an uninhabited area under 100 kilometers away from Apo Island.<ref name="Eco Tipping Points">{{cite web |title=Marine Sanctuary: Restoring a Coral-Reef Fishery (Apo Island, Philippines) {{!}} The EcoTipping Points Project |url=http://www.ecotippingpoints.org/our-stories/indepth/philippines-apo-marine-sanctuary-coral-reef-fishery.html |website=www.ecotippingpoints.org}}</ref> Another research element Alcala incorporated in his study is associating the species’ survival rate of large, predatory fish with available ocean territories around reefs and [[fisheries]]. This helped place an effort to set boundaries to distinguish marine sanctuaries and fishing areas. Alcala's conservation efforts accompanied by his research in oceanic and land management helped stabilize retention of once-endangered species in the [[Sumilon Island]] and Apo Island marine reserves.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Russ |first1=Garry R. |last2=Alcala |first2=Angel C. |title=Marine Reserves: Rates and Patterns of Recovery and Decline of Large Predatory Fish |journal=Ecological Applications |date=August 1, 1996 |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=947–961 |doi=10.2307/2269497 |jstor=2269497 |url=https://researchonline.jcu.edu.au/1464/1/Russ_and_Alcala_2003.pdf }}</ref>

His studies correlated the efforts of protective environmental practices with the effects of either continuing or ceasing those regulations. Incidents of fishing are common consequences when ocean space and resources are available and not properly managed. These studies were primarily conducted near [[coral reefs]] of Sumilon Island located in the central Philippines. Alcala concluded how maximizing conservation and environmental efforts near these coral reefs reduced fishing and stabilized struggling fish species that faced the increased loss of habitat.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Russ |first1=G. R. |last2=Alcala |first2=A. C. |title=A direct test of the effects of protective management on abundance and yield of tropical marine resources |journal=Journal du Conseil International pour l'Exploration de la Mer |date=January 1, 1990 |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=40–47 |doi=10.1093/icesjms/47.1.40}}</ref>

===Marine conservation===

Angel Alcala experimented with his teams to conserve coral reefs and other marine resources. In their "no-take" experiment,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abesamis |first1=Rene A. |last2=Russ |first2=Garry R. |last3=Alcala |first3=Angel C. |title=Gradients of abundance of fish across no-take marine reserve boundaries: evidence from Philippine coral reefs |journal=Aquatic Conservation: Marine and Freshwater Ecosystems |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=349–371 |doi=10.1002/aqc.730 |date=2006}}</ref> Alcala's team tested the mobility of fish species when humans were forbidden from fishing in these areas. By doing so, they discovered that the [[species]] abundance in the area declined while pushing the boundaries of their residence to further reaches. These findings provide evidence that conservation of these fishes and coral reefs not only slows the species' decline in numbers, but also the growth in habitat for all marine life.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Russ |first1=G. R. |last2=Alcala |first2=A. C. |title=Management histories of Sumilon and Apo Marine Reserves, Philippines, and their influence on national marine resource policy |issue=4 |journal=Coral Reefs |volume=18 |pages=307–319 |doi=10.1007/s003380050203 |date=December 1, 1999|s2cid=8912347 }}</ref>

[[File:Bolinao Giant Clam Sanctuary.jpg|thumb|Bolinao Giant Clam Sanctuary]]
Alcala has also worked to protect the lives of [[giant clam]]s in the Philippines. He worked alongside Dr. Edgardo Gomez to assess the organisms' status in 1983. After thorough evaluation of [[Bolinao, Pangasinan|Bolinao]] waters, they learned that the numbers were insufficient. Gomez and Alcala retrieved young giant clams from the [[Solomon Islands]] to breed back in Bolinao. After their work, the giant clam population has increased significantly to ensure that the ecosystem is stable.<ref name="Giant Clam Fam">{{cite news |last1=Cabigao |first1=Stephanie |title=Meet the giant clam fam |url=https://www.up.edu.ph/index.php/meet-the-giant-clam-fam/ |work=University of the Philippines |date=June 22, 2018}}</ref> On October 25, 2014, he visited the [[Semirara]] coast where he spoke in favor of saving giant clams.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://business.inquirer.net/180899/spawning-giant-clams-for-livelihood |title=Spawning giant clams for livelihood |publisher=[[Inquirer.net]] |date=October 25, 2014 |access-date=October 28, 2014 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141028025713/http://business.inquirer.net/180899/spawning-giant-clams-for-livelihood |archivedate=October 28, 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Species discoveries===
Along with his many other accomplishments, Angel Alcala's work has led to the discovery of 50 new species of reptiles and amphibians.<ref name="ASEAN">{{cite web |title=ASEAN Biodiversity Hero – Dr. Angel C. Alcala, Philippines – ASEAN Biodiversity Heroes |url=http://heroes.aseanbiodiversity.org/2017/09/07/asean-biodiversity-hero-dr-angel-c-alcala-philippines/ |website=heroes.aseanbiodiversity.org}}</ref> In other words, more than 10 percent of all reptiles and amphibians in the Philippines are known today because of Alcala's work. This fieldwork began while he was still a student and ultimately built a stronger foundation to jumpstart conservation programs within the Philippines.<ref name="BusinessMirror">{{cite news |last1=Mayuga |first1=Jonathan L. |title=Dr. Angel Alcala is PHL's biodiversity hero |url=https://businessmirror.com.ph/dr-angel-alcala-is-phls-biodiversity-hero/ |work=BusinessMirror |date=August 13, 2017}}</ref>

==Awards and other accomplishments==
In 1959, Angel Alcala earned the Fulbright-Smith Mundt master's fellowship in [[Stanford University]]'s biology department.<ref name="FULBRIGHT">{{cite news|url=https://fulbright.org.ph/angel-alcala-named-national-scientist |title=Angel Alcala named National Scientist {{!}} Fulbright Commission in the Philippines|date=December 12, 2013|agency=FULBRIGHT Philippine-American Education Foundation}}</ref>

In 1963, Alcala was awarded the [https://www.gf.org/about/fellowship/ Guggenheim Fellowship for Natural Sciences] in the category for Organismal Biology & Ecology.

In 1992, the [[Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation]] awarded Alcala the [[Ramon Magsaysay Award]] and acknowledged him for pioneering scientific leadership in restoring and conserving the coral reefs of the Philippines.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rmaward.asia/awardees/alcala-angel-chua/ |title=Alcala, Angel Chua |work=Awardees |publisher=Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation |access-date=March 3, 2021}}</ref>

In 1994, he received the [https://www.fieldmuseum.org/join-give/groups/founders-council Field Museum Founders' Council Award of Merit] for his contributions to environmental biology.

In 1999, he was awarded the Pew Fellowship in Marine Conservation for his continued, exceptional work in marine conservation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pew Fellows Program in Marine Conservation Awards: Mission |url=https://www.pewtrusts.org/en/projects/marine-fellows/about |website=pew.org}}</ref>

In 2014, [[President of the Philippines|President]] [[Benigno Simeon Aquino III]] Proclamation No. 782, naming Alcala a National Scientist of the Philippines<ref>{{cite news|title=Palace names 2 National Scientists |publisher=[[The Philippine Star]] |date=June 12, 2014 |url=http://www.philstar.com/science-and-technology/2014/06/12/1333648/palace-names-2-national-scientists |access-date=June 12, 2014 |author=Aurea Calica |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140615145853/http://www.philstar.com/science-and-technology/2014/06/12/1333648/palace-names-2-national-scientists |archivedate=June 15, 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref> in recognition of his research on ecology and diversity of Philippine amphibians and reptiles, marine biodiversity, and marine-protected areas.

In 2017, Alcala was named an ASEAN Biodiversity Hero.<ref name="ASEAN" /> He was also previously the [[Department of Environment and Natural Resources]] (DENR) Secretary in the Philippines.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Miguel |first1=Claire |title=Ex-DENR chief named among ASEAN Biodiversity Heroes hailed |url=https://www.denr.gov.ph/news-and-features/latest-news/3231-ex-denr-chief-named-among-asean-biodiversity-heroes-hailed.html |website=www.denr.gov.ph }}</ref>

In 2018, he was named a member of the Fulbright Philippines Hall of Fame.<ref name="Silliman University" />

In November 2018, he was awarded Oceans Legend by PEMSEA during the East Asian Seas (EAS) Congress in Iloilo City.

In 2022, he was added to the [[Asian Scientist 100]] by ''[[Asian Scientist]]''.

Two species of Philippine snakes are named in his honor: ''[[Lycodon alcalai]]'' and ''[[Opisthotropis|Opisthotropis alcalai]]''.<ref>[[species:Bo Beolens|Beolens, Bo]]; [[species:Michael Watkins|Watkins, Michael]]; Grayson, Michael (2011). ''The Eponym Dictionary of Reptiles''. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. xiii + 296 pp. {{ISBN|978-1-4214-0135-5}}. (Alcala, p. 4).</ref>

One species of nudibranch is named in his honor: ''[[Chromodoris alcalai]]''.<ref>Gosliner, T.M. (2020) Sleuthing cryptic Chromodorids (Mollusca, Nudibranchia): adding to Philippine marine biodiversity. Philippine Journal of Systematic Biology, Volume 14, Issue 2. DOI 10.26757/pjsb2020b14014</ref>

== Private life and death ==
Alcala was married to Naomi and they had 6 children.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=National Academy of Science and Technology Philippines |last2=Primavera |first2=Jurgenne |date=August 2023 |title=Angel C. Alcala — Grand Old Man of Philippine Marine Science |url=https://transactions.nast.ph/?p=3320 |journal=Transactions of the National Academy of Science and Technology |volume=45 |issue=2023 |pages=1–23 |doi=10.57043/transnastphl.2023.3320|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Alcala died on February 1, 2023, at the age of 93.<ref>[https://www.abs-cbn.com/news/02/01/23/national-scientist-angel-alcala-dies-at-93 National Scientist Angel Alcala passes away at 93]</ref>
